lastText: File ClosedAnswering, Never AskingMajor DefeatWehrmacht High Command, 1939–1945End of hostilities: MARCH 1945 (PROJECTED) · filed out of sequence, pages missingImmediate AftermathThe end comes early, around March 1945: the calendar itself the clearest casualty of this path's decisions. What surrenders at the end is less an army than a casualty ledger with a rear echelon. And it ended immobile: whatever strength remained stood where it stood, out of fuel, defending only what it could walk to. So little organized force remained by the end that both Allied advances accelerated freely: the final meeting line lands wherever logistics, not resistance, decided. Sea Lion was actually launched, the September crossing every staff study warned against, and the army fought the rest of the war missing the assault divisions it left on English shingle. Sixth Army left the Volga as an army: the single largest body of men any decision in this campaign moves from the dead column to the living. One thread runs the full length of this campaign back to May 1940: pressing the attack at Dunkirk thinned the veteran leadership Britain historically rebuilt around: a quiet effect, still present in the British sector a dozen decisions later. Holding the last panzer reserve on the Oder rather than spending it in Hungary made the final defense of Berlin slower and costlier for the attackers: the war's last decision, decided against its historical grain.
